writeup.1: The bar is narrow on purpose: founded in Texas, and still based in Texas. That cuts the brands putting a longhorn on a hat from an office in California, and it cuts the companies that opened a Dallas warehouse and started calling themselves Texan.
writeup.2: Sixteen clear it, and they have startlingly little in common. Clint Orms has been hand-engraving silver in Kerrville since 1992 and will not reproduce more than ten pieces from any one design. Ally Aiken painted a course map for her husband in 2020 and now has hundreds of courses in the catalogue. Harry and Zach wrap leather grips in Conroe as a father-and-son shop, Scott Matthews left investment banking in New York for Dallas over a polyester polo, and Mike Taylor and John Hatfield came off the Nike payroll on a Friday and opened Artisan in the same Fort Worth building on the Monday.
writeup.3: That last one is the closest thing to a pattern. When Nike left the golf equipment business in 2016 it left behind a ten-thousand-square-foot building in Fort Worth and a group of people who knew how to grind a wedge, and two of the best club shops in the country grew out of the vacancy. P53 leases its space in that same building from Marty Leonard, whose father Marvin built Colonial. Ben Hogan is buried in the city. The metal work clusters where it does for a reason.
writeup.4: One distinction matters in the apparel section: designed in Texas and made in Texas are not the same claim. Criquet designs at its Clubhouse in Austin and prints made in Peru on the Players Shirt. Artisan prints made in Fort Worth on the building. Both are fine, and the good ones say which is which on the product page.
